questions.stem: Which parts make up the structure of a transformer?

options.text: primary coil, secondary coil and iron core
options.explanation: These three are the transformer's structure.

options.text: a single coil and a permanent magnet
options.explanation: Transformers need two coils and no permanent magnet.
Those belong to motors and dynamos.

options.text: a battery and a plastic core
options.explanation: Neither belongs in a transformer's structure.

questions.stem: Which coil of a transformer is connected to the input supply?

options.text: neither — the core carries the input
options.explanation: The core carries the field, not the input connection.
Primary takes the input; secondary gives the output.
The secondary delivers the induced output.

options.text: both coils share the input equally
options.explanation: Input and output are separate windings.

questions.stem: A transformer is supplied with steady direct voltage. The secondary output is:

options.explanation: A steady input gives no output at all.
Turns ratio cannot rescue a non-changing field.

options.text: zero, because the core field is not changing
options.explanation: Induction needs a changing field through the secondary.
No change, no induction, no output.

questions.stem: What does a transformer change about its input?

options.explanation: The output alternates at the same frequency as the input.
Transformers pass alternating output; rectifiers make DC.
Transformers transfer energy; they do not create it.

options.text: the size of the alternating voltage
options.explanation: The turns ratio sets the output voltage size.

questions.stem: Why must the input to a transformer be alternating?

options.text: the secondary only induces while the core field keeps changing
options.explanation: A changing field is the induction trigger.

options.text: direct current would melt the primary coil
options.explanation: Heating is not the reason transformers need AC.

options.text: the iron core only carries alternating fields
options.explanation: The core carries any field; only CHANGE induces.

options.text: the turns ratio only works for AC voltages
options.explanation: The ratio is geometry; the AC need is induction itself.

questions.stem: State the three structural parts of a transformer.
questions.modelAnswer: A primary coil, a secondary coil, and a shared iron core.

questions.stem: State what kind of supply a transformer requires and why.
questions.modelAnswer: An alternating supply, because the secondary only has a voltage induced while the core's field is changing.

questions.stem: Explain how the input voltage's change reaches the secondary coil.
questions.modelAnswer: The alternating current in the primary makes the core's magnetic field grow and shrink continuously. That changing field threads every turn of the secondary coil, and a changing field through a coil induces a voltage across it — so the primary's alternating behaviour is relayed to the secondary as an induced alternating output.

questions.stem: A student connects a battery to a transformer's primary and a meter to its secondary. State the meter reading at switch-on, after it settles, and at switch-off — and explain the pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: At switch-on the field through the core changes for a moment, so the meter kicks briefly; while the battery holds steady the field stops changing and the meter reads zero; at switch-off the field collapses, giving a brief kick the other way. Only CHANGES in the core field induce — steady DC gives steady zero.

questions.stem: A transformer has more turns on the secondary than on the primary. It is a:

options.text: transformer with equal input and output voltages
options.explanation: Equal voltages need equal turns.
More secondary turns raise the output voltage.
Step-down needs fewer secondary turns.
Dynamos rotate; transformers are static.

questions.stem: What happens to the output voltage when the primary has 200 turns and the secondary has 50?

options.explanation: Equal voltages need equal turns.
Fewer turns lower the voltage; they do not remove it.

options.text: it is stepped down to a quarter of the input
options.explanation: 50/200 is a quarter — fewer output turns, lower voltage.
That reads the ratio backwards.

questions.stem: Which quantity passes through a transformer unchanged?

options.explanation: Changing voltage size is the transformer's whole job.
The two coils have different turns by design.
Different windings have different resistances.

options.text: the frequency of the alternating voltage
options.explanation: The core field alternates at the input frequency.

questions.stem: A mains adapter must convert 230 V to a safe low voltage for a toy. Which transformer suits?

options.text: a step-down transformer with fewer secondary turns
options.explanation: Lowering the voltage needs fewer output turns.

options.text: a step-up transformer with more secondary turns
options.explanation: That would raise the already-high mains voltage.
Generators make electricity from motion; adapters transform it.

options.text: a transformer with equal turns on both coils
options.explanation: Equal turns leave the voltage unchanged at 230 V.

questions.stem: The turns on a transformer's secondary are increased while the primary is untouched. The output voltage:

options.explanation: Adding turns never cancels the output.

options.text: increases in proportion to the added turns
options.explanation: Output scales with the secondary turn count.
More secondary turns raise the output.
The output stays alternating regardless of turns.

questions.stem: State the turns relationship in a step-up transformer.
questions.modelAnswer: A step-up transformer carries more turns on its secondary winding than on its primary.

questions.stem: State what happens to the frequency of the voltage across a transformer.
questions.modelAnswer: The frequency is unchanged: the output alternates at the same rate as the input.

questions.stem: Explain why equal turns on both coils give an output equal to the input.
questions.modelAnswer: The changing core field induces the same voltage per turn in both windings, because both share the identical field. With equal numbers of turns, the same per-turn voltage is summed the same number of times on each side, so the output matches the input voltage — the turns ratio of one passes the size through unchanged.

questions.stem: Two transformers run from the same 12 V AC supply: one steps up to 48 V, the other steps down to 3 V. Compare their turns ratios and classify each.
questions.modelAnswer: The 48 V unit has four times the primary turns on its secondary — a 4:1 secondary-to-primary ratio — so it is a step-up transformer. The 3 V unit has a quarter of the primary turns on its secondary — a 1:4 ratio — so it is a step-down transformer.

questions.stem: Why is electricity transmitted across the grid at very high voltage?

options.text: high voltage is required by the transformers only
options.explanation: Transformers set the voltage; the REASON is the heat saving.

options.text: electricity travels faster at high voltage
options.explanation: Speed is not the reason; heating is.

options.text: the lower current then wastes less energy as heat in the cables
options.explanation: High voltage means low current for the same power.

options.text: high voltage makes the cables stronger
options.explanation: Voltage does not change cable mechanics.

questions.stem: Which transformer sits at the power-station end of the grid?

options.explanation: Step-down units sit at the consumer end.
The generator makes the electricity; the transformer raises the voltage.

options.text: no transformer — the generator outputs the grid voltage
options.explanation: Step-up transformers bridge generator and grid.
The voltage is raised before the long journey.

questions.stem: What do step-down transformers do near consumers?

options.text: lower the transmission voltage to safe levels
options.explanation: Step-down units make the supply usable and safe.

options.text: raise the voltage for the cables
options.explanation: That is the step-up role at the station.

options.text: convert AC to DC for homes
options.explanation: Homes receive AC; rectification is separate.
Transformers transfer; they do not store.

questions.stem: For the same transmitted power, raising the transmission voltage tenfold makes the cable current:

options.explanation: Current falls but never to zero while power flows.
Power = voltage × current, so current falls with rising voltage.
That inverts the power relationship.
Current and voltage trade off at fixed power.

questions.stem: Lower current in the transmission cables means:

options.explanation: Current is what heats the cables.
The transmitted power is fixed; only the split changes.

options.text: less energy wasted heating the cables
options.explanation: Cable heating falls sharply as current falls.

options.text: more energy wasted in the cables
options.explanation: The loss falls with the current.

questions.stem: State which transformer type raises the voltage for transmission.
questions.modelAnswer: A step-up transformer raises the voltage at the power-station end of the grid.

questions.stem: State why a lower cable current is wanted on the grid.
questions.modelAnswer: A lower current wastes less energy as heat in the transmission cables.

questions.stem: Explain the full chain from step-up transformer to cooler cables.
questions.modelAnswer: The step-up transformer raises the transmission voltage, so for the same transmitted power the current in the cables is lower. Cable heating is caused by the current, so the reduced current wastes less energy as heat — more of the generated power reaches the consumer end, where step-down transformers restore a safe voltage.

questions.stem: A grid link loses noticeable energy as cable heat. The operators raise the transmission voltage using stronger step-up transformers. Describe and explain the change in the link's losses.
questions.modelAnswer: The losses fall. With the transmitted power fixed, the higher voltage lets the same power flow at a lower current, and it is the current that heats the cables. The reduced current therefore wastes less energy as cable heat, so more of the generated energy arrives at the far end.
